attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated as his own view.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the $718B figure, the dependence on venture funding, and the 'because' premise. The causal kind fits the 'because' link.

contract.note: Reading 'lose money on every transaction' as negative unit economics (gross margin) is an ordinary reading of per-transaction losses. It is not stretched. Pinning the claim to Q1 2026 fits a present-tense statement. The outcome depends on this reading, because Anthropic's operating loss and need for funding in Q1 are not in dispute.

evidence.note: S-1 quarterly table: Q1 2026 revenue was $4,731M against $3,387M of total compute, which also covers research. So serving customers cost less than it earned. This is an unaudited company filing.
Confirms that the compute line includes research and training, so the cost of serving customers alone was lower still.
Positive gross margins in FY2025 and H1 2026. These periods differ from the Q1 2026 target, so this is corroborating context only.
Partial tally of Anthropic's vendor commitments (Google, Amazon, Microsoft about $270B). It does not cover OpenAI, so it does not verify $718B.

reviews.rationale: The causal premise is that the businesses lose money on every transaction, read as negative gross margin. The S-1 refutes this for Anthropic in Q1 2026: revenue exceeded all compute spending, including research. Under the contract, refuting the premise for either company falsifies the claim. Anthropic's operating loss and fundraising (needs funding) are not contradicted, and the $718B figure and OpenAI were not checked. But the stated cause fails.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'I think', the lying charge and the mathematical reason. 'I think' frames an opinion, but the factual premise it implies is firm: the $4.5B 2025 figure was false and arithmetically impossible.

contract.note: Intent cannot be tested, so grading the arithmetic premise is fair. One flaw: the affidavit is dated March 2026, but the 'just over $5B' match uses lifetime revenue through December 2025. Even so, 'exceeding $5B' has no upper bound and so does not conflict with $4.5B in 2025. The outcome does not depend on this.

evidence.note: Audited S-1: 2025 revenue was $4,585M, which is about $4.5B. So the sources' figure was accurate. Note that the derived $5.0B lifetime figure runs through December 2025, not to the March 2026 affidavit date.
Confirms that the 2023–2025 figures come from audited statements.

reviews.rationale: The claim implies the reported $4.5B 2025 revenue figure was false and mathematically impossible. Audited S-1 figures show 2025 revenue of $4,585M, so the figure was correct. A lifetime total 'exceeding $5 billion' by March 2026 fits it. His mathematical basis fails, and so does his charge that the sources lied. Whether anyone intended to deceive cannot be tested.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition matches his words. The graded part, 'no path to profitability', is a firm judgment about the future ('even clearer'). It works as an open-horizon forecast, not a pure observation. The 'weird things' part has no standard.

contract.note: Treating positive GAAP operating income as profitability of the business is an ordinary reading. Anthropic's huge net loss comes from non-cash fair-value charges on convertible notes, not from operations. A net-income reading would change the result, so the interpretation matters. The early-resolution rule (one positive operating quarter for either company) is reasonable for 'both of them'.

evidence.note: Quarterly revenue growth to $11.6B in Q2 2026. Background only.
S-1 shows $974M GAAP operating income for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, after the post. This meets the early-resolution rule. Unaudited company filing.
Defines Anthropic's run-rate method. Bears on 'weird things', which is not graded.

reviews.rationale: Anthropic reported positive GAAP operating income ($974M) for Q2 2026, a dated event disclosed before the evaluation date. This meets the early-resolution rule, so the claim that neither company has a path to profitability is contradicted. 'Weird things with annualized revenues' has no testable standard and is not scored. OpenAI was not reviewed, but that does not matter given the claim covers both.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'if truly capacity constrained' antecedent, customer growth and the two-nines threshold. 'Greed' and 'choosing' are normative overlay.

contract.note: Reading 'struggles to keep above two nines' as main-service uptime near or below 99% is ordinary. So is the 90-day window ending on the post date. condition_status says not_applicable even though there is an antecedent, but the evidence shows the antecedent was met. The moral judgments are rightly left ungraded.

evidence.note: Archived status page on the post date: claude.ai at 98.73% over 90 days, with the API, Console and Code just above 99%. Company-measured, and against its own interest.
Anthropic says customers spending over $1M doubled from February to April 2026. This counts large business customers only, but it shows customer growth in the window.
Independent dated report of outages and peak-hour limits as usage grew. Supports the capacity-crunch antecedent.
S-1 says Anthropic has consistently been compute-constrained, which supports the antecedent. Company disclosure, filed before the evaluation date.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent held: the S-1 and Fortune both show a real compute crunch. In the window, Anthropic added customers (large business accounts doubled), and 90-day uptime was below 99% for claude.ai and barely above it for the API, Console and Code. That fits 'struggles to keep above two nines'. The charge of 'greed' and the claim it was 'choosing' this are moral judgments and were not scored.
